about.p: This course covers the grammar that intermediate learners most need – and most often get wrong: tenses, modal verbs, conditionals, the passive, reported speech, articles, relative clauses, prepositions and much more. Each unit explains one point clearly, with plenty of examples in natural British English, and ends with exercises that check you can really use it.

The units are grouped by topic, but they are not in order of difficulty. Choose the units you need, or work through a whole section – for example all the units on the present perfect – to see how the forms fit together.

about.-: Read the explanation and say the examples aloud. Watch the *Common mistake* boxes: they show the errors learners make most often.
Do the exercises without looking back at the explanation. A wrong answer comes back after 1, 3, 7 and 16 days until you get it right.
Finish each unit by writing a few sentences about your own life with the grammar you have just studied.

about.tip: Grammar sticks when you use it. After a unit, try to use its structure three times that day – in a message, a conversation or your diary.

L.p: Make the present continuous with *am/is/are* + the *-ing* form of the verb. In conversation we normally use the short forms *I'm*, *you're*, *she's*, *it's* and so on.

L.tip: Spelling: make → making, write → writing, stop → stopping, sit → sitting, lie → lying, die → dying.

L.p: Use the present continuous for an action that is in progress at the moment of speaking: it has started, and it has not finished yet.

L.e: Please be quiet – the baby's sleeping. 'Where's Dad?' 'In the garden. He's cutting the grass.' Look! It's starting to snow. You aren't listening to a word I'm saying!

L.x: I *am writing* (not *I writing*) to you from a café in Madrid.

L.p: We also use it for something that is in progress around the present – today, this week, these days – even if it is not happening at the exact moment we speak.

L.e: I'm watching a brilliant series at the moment – I'm on episode six. (I'm not watching it now: I'm talking to you.) Sam's working in a café until he finds a better job. Are you revising for your exams this week?

L.p: Use the present continuous with verbs such as *get*, *change*, *rise*, *fall*, *improve* and *grow* to describe situations that are changing now.

L.e: The days are getting longer. Prices are rising every month. Dad's cooking is getting better – he's taking lessons. More and more people are working from home.

L.x: Look – the bus *is coming* (not *comes*)! Run!

X.i: Choose the correct form.

units.O: Write five sentences about your life at the moment: your work or studies, what you are reading or watching, and something that is changing.
units.sub: am/is/are + -ing for things happening now or around now

L.p: The present simple is the base form of the verb, with *-s* after *he*, *she* and *it*. Questions and negatives use *do/does* + the base form.

L.tip: Spelling after he/she/it: watch → watches, finish → finishes, go → goes, do → does, study → studies, carry → carries, have → has.

L.x: My sister *doesn't like* (not *don't like*) spicy food.
*Does he speak* (not *Does he speaks*) French?

L.p: Use the present simple for things that are true in general, and for things that happen again and again: habits, routines and timetables.

L.e: Water freezes at 0 °C. My sister works for a bank in Edinburgh. I don't drink coffee after six o'clock. The shops close at half past five on Sundays. How many times a week do you train?

L.p: Words like *always*, *usually*, *often*, *sometimes*, *hardly ever* and *never* go with the present simple. They normally come before the main verb but after *be*.

L.e: I always walk to work. We hardly ever eat out. She checks her phone every five minutes. He's never late.

L.p: Sometimes the present simple itself does what it says: when you say *I promise*, you are promising. The same is true of *I suggest*, *I apologise*, *I agree* and *I refuse*.

L.e: I promise to be careful with your car. I suggest we leave early to avoid the traffic. I apologise for the delay. 'It's too expensive.' 'I agree.'

units.sub: habits, facts and things that are always true

L.p: Use the *present continuous* for actions in progress now or in the period around now, and the *present simple* for facts and for things that happen in general or again and again.

t: The kettle's boiling – shall I make the tea?
Why are you wearing a coat? It's warm today.
I always wear a coat in winter.

L.x: Be quiet, please. I *am trying* (not *try*) to work.

L.p: Use the present continuous for a situation that you see as temporary. Use the present simple for one that you see as permanent or long-term.

L.e: I'm living with my parents until I find a flat. My parents live in a village near York. Jack's working nights this month. Jack works for an engineering company.

L.h: C always with the present continuous

L.p: *always* with the present continuous means 'too often' or 'more often than usual'. We often use it to complain. Compare the present simple, where *always* means 'every time'.

L.e: You're always leaving the lights on! He's always interrupting me when I'm talking. I always lose at chess. (= every time I play)

L.x: You *are always leaving* (not *always are leaving*) the door open!

units.sub: now and temporary or always and permanent

L.h: A Verbs we don't usually use in the continuous

L.p: Some verbs describe states, not actions, so we normally use them in the simple form, even for 'now'. Common ones are *like, love, hate, want, need, prefer, know, realise, suppose, mean, understand, believe, remember, belong, fit, contain, consist* and *seem*.

L.e: I'm thirsty. I need a drink. Do you know the way to the station? I don't believe a word he says. This soup needs more salt. The house seems empty without the dog.

L.x: I *know* (not *am knowing*) the answer.
This box *contains* (not *is containing*) old photos.

L.p: When *think* means 'believe' or 'have an opinion', use the simple form. When it means 'consider' or 'use your mind', you can use the continuous.

L.e: I think you're right. Do you think the shop is still open? I'm thinking about changing jobs. Be quiet – I'm thinking!

L.h: C see, hear, smell, taste, look and feel

L.p: *see*, *hear*, *smell* and *taste* are usually simple, and we often use *can* with them. When *taste* or *smell* is an action, you can use the continuous. With *look* (= seem) and *feel* (= how you are), both forms are possible.

L.e: I can see the sea from my window. This milk smells strange. The chef is tasting the sauce. You look tired. / You're looking well. How do you feel? / How are you feeling?

L.h: D he is being / he is

L.p: *I'm being*, *he's being* and so on mean 'behaving' or 'acting' at a particular time. Compare *he is*, which describes his character.

L.e: You're being very generous today. (= you are acting generously) He's generous. (= that is his character) Why is she being so quiet? Is something wrong?

L.p: Regular verbs add *-ed* in the past simple: *work → worked*, *arrive → arrived*. Many common verbs are irregular, and you need to learn their past forms. The past simple has the same form for every person: *I went*, *she went*, *they went*.

L.tip: Spelling: stop → stopped, plan → planned, try → tried, study → studied, live → lived, travel → travelled (British English).

L.p: Use *did* + the base form for questions and *didn't* + the base form for negatives. Don't use the past form after *did*.

L.e: Did you enjoy the concert? Where did they spend their honeymoon? I didn't recognise her at first. We didn't have time to stop.

L.x: *Did you see* (not *Did you saw*) the match last night?
I *didn't go* (not *didn't went*) out at the weekend.

L.p: Use the past simple for actions and situations that are finished. We often say when they happened: *yesterday*, *last week*, *in 2015*, *three days ago*, *when I was a child*.

L.e: My grandparents met in 1968. I lost my wallet on the bus yesterday. We didn't own a car when I was little. When did you start learning English?

L.p: The past of *be* is *was* (I/he/she/it) and *were* (we/you/they). Questions and negatives don't use *did*.

L.e: I was exhausted after the flight. Were you at home last night? The roads weren't very busy. Why was she so upset?

units.O: Write about last weekend: where you went, who you saw, what you ate and what you didn't have time to do.
units.sub: finished actions in the past; regular and irregular verbs

L.p: Make the past continuous with *was/were* + *-ing*.

L.x: When I phoned, they *were* (not *was*) having lunch.

L.h: B In the middle of something

L.p: Use the past continuous for an action that was in progress at a particular time in the past. It had started before that time and had not finished.

L.e: At eight o'clock last night I was watching a film. What were you doing when the lights went out? This time last year we were living in Leeds. It was a beautiful morning: the birds were singing and the sun was shining.

L.h: C Past continuous and past simple together

L.p: We often use the two tenses together: the past continuous for the longer background action, and the past simple for a shorter action that happened in the middle of it. Use the past simple alone for actions that happened one after another.

L.e: I was chopping onions when I cut my finger. While we were walking home, it started to rain. When Sara arrived, we were having dinner. (= dinner had already started) When Sara arrived, we had dinner. (= first she arrived, then we ate)

L.p: State verbs such as *know*, *want*, *believe* and *belong* don't usually take the continuous form (see Unit 4), so we use the past simple with them.

L.e: I didn't know where I was. Everybody wanted to go home.

L.x: We were exhausted, so we *wanted* (not *were wanting*) to go home.

L.p: Make the present perfect with *have/has* + the past participle. Regular verbs have the same form for the past simple and the past participle (*worked*, *arrived*). Many common verbs have irregular past participles.

L.h: B A past action with a result now

L.p: Use the present perfect when something happened in the past but you are thinking about the result now. We often use it to give new information. We don't say exactly when it happened.

L.e: I've lost my keys. (= I don't have them now) The lift has broken down, so we'll have to take the stairs. Look! Somebody has painted the front door. Have you heard? Mia's got a new job.

L.p: *just* = a short time ago. *already* = sooner than expected. *yet* = until now, in questions and negatives; it goes at the end of the sentence.

L.e: I've just made some tea – would you like a cup? We've already seen this film. Has the post come yet? I haven't decided yet.

L.x: Have you finished the report *yet* (not *already yet*)?

L.p: *She has gone to Spain* means she is in Spain now, or on her way there. *She has been to Spain* means she went there and has come back.

L.e: 'Where's Max?' 'He's gone to the bank. He'll be back in ten minutes.' 'You look brown!' 'I've been to Greece for a week.'

L.x: My brother *has gone* (not *has been*) to the shops – he'll be back soon.

units.O: Write about recent changes in your life or your town. What has happened? What has changed? Use just, already and yet.
units.sub: a past action with a result now; just, already, yet

L.p: The present perfect is used for experiences in your life up to now. We often use *ever* in questions and *never* in negative statements, and we don't say when the experience happened.

L.e: Have you ever eaten octopus? I've never been to Scotland. My aunt has travelled all over Africa. It's the most beautiful beach I've ever seen.

L.x: I *have never seen* (not *never have seen*) such a big dog.

L.h: B A period that continues until now

L.p: Use it with a period of time that is not finished: *today*, *this morning*, *this week*, *this year*, *recently*, *so far*, *in the last few days*.

L.e: I've had three phone calls from the bank today. Have you been away at all this summer? We haven't seen Tom recently. So far we've raised £500 for the hospital.

L.p: After *It's the first time*, *It's the second time* and so on, use the present perfect.

L.e: It's the first time she's flown business class. It's the second time you've been late this week. Is it the first time your parents have visited Wales?

L.x: It's the first time I *have tried* (not *try*) snowboarding.

L.p: Make the present perfect continuous with *have/has been* + *-ing*.

L.h: B An activity that has just stopped

L.p: Use it for an activity that went on for a period and has recently stopped. Often we can see or feel the result now.

L.e: The kitchen smells of garlic – have you been cooking? Sorry I'm so hot. I've been cycling up the hill. Your hands are covered in paint. Have you been decorating?

L.h: C An activity that is still going on

L.p: Use it with *how long*, *for* and *since* when the activity started in the past and hasn't stopped yet.

L.e: We've been waiting for the bus for twenty minutes. How long have you been learning Korean? It's been snowing since early this morning. She's been working at the hospital since 2019.

L.x: I *have been waiting* (not *am waiting*) here for an hour.
How long *have you been learning* (not *are you learning*) English?

L.h: D Actions repeated over a period

L.p: You can also use it for actions that have happened again and again over a period up to now.

L.e: He's been playing chess every Thursday since he retired. I've been having a lot of headaches lately. The neighbours have been arguing all week.

units.O: Write about three activities in your life that started in the past and are still going on. How long have you been doing them?
units.t: Present perfect continuous (I have been doing)
units.sub: an activity that has recently stopped or is still going on

L.h: A The activity or the result?

L.p: The continuous form puts the focus on the activity – it may or may not be over. The simple form puts the focus on the completed result.

L.e: I've been writing my essay all morning. (= the activity; it may not be finished) I've written my essay – here it is. (= it is finished) She's been tidying her room. She's tidied her room, so now you can see the floor.

L.h: B How long, or how much and how many?

L.p: Ask or answer *how long* with the continuous form. When you count – *how much*, *how many*, *how many times* – use the simple form, because you are talking about what has been completed.

L.e: Lucy has been reading since lunch – she's already read half the book. How long has your dad been driving? How many times have you driven to Scotland? They've been playing tennis since lunchtime. They've played four sets.

L.x: I've *written* (not *been writing*) three emails this morning.

L.h: C Verbs that are not used in the continuous

L.p: State verbs such as *know*, *have* (= own) and *believe* take the simple form, even when you say how long.

L.e: How long has your brother had his motorbike? We've known each other since school. I've always believed in second chances.

L.x: I've *known* (not *been knowing*) Sam since primary school.

X.i: Simple or continuous? Choose the better form.

units.sub: how long (continuous) or how much and how many (simple)

L.h: A Now, but it started in the past

L.p: For a situation that started in the past and is still true now, English uses the present perfect – not the present simple. *how long*, *for* and *since* often go with it.

L.e: My parents are retired. They've been retired for six years. 'Is he ill?' 'Yes, he's been ill since Sunday.' How long have you two been together?

L.x: I *have lived* (not *live*) here since 2015.

L.p: For actions, the continuous is usual. With *live* and *work* you can use either form. With *always*, use the simple.

L.e: How long have you been playing the violin? Sara has worked / has been working here for a year. I've always lived in this town.

L.p: With state verbs like *know*, *have* (= own or suffer from) and *be*, use the simple form.

L.e: How long have you known Leo? I've had a headache since lunchtime. She's been a nurse for fifteen years.

L.p: Use a negative present perfect to say how long it is since something happened.

L.e: I haven't seen my cousins for months. We haven't had a proper holiday since 2021. She hasn't eaten anything since breakfast.

units.O: Write about the people and things in your life now – your home, job, friends and hobbies – and say how long each has been part of your life.
units.sub: a situation that began in the past and continues now

L.p: *for* tells you the length of a period: *for two hours*, *for a week*, *for ages*. *since* tells you when the period started: *since Monday*, *since 2010*, *since I was a child*.

L.e: I've been sitting here for forty minutes. The museum has been closed since March. She's lived abroad since she finished university. We waited for an hour, then went home.

L.x: I've lived here *for* (not *since*) six years.

L.p: *ago* goes after a period of time and means 'before now'. It goes with the past simple; don't use it with the present perfect.

L.e: I started this job three years ago. The plane landed twenty minutes ago. How long ago did your grandparents come to Britain?

L.x: We moved here three years *ago* (not *before*).

L.p: You can also say *It's* (= it is or it has been) + a period + *since* + the past simple.

L.e: It's eight months since my sister last phoned. (= she hasn't rung me for eight months) It's been ages since we last went out for a meal. How long has it been since you had a day off?

L.p: Ask *When …?* with the past simple about a point in the past. Ask *How long …?* with the present perfect about a period up to now.

L.e: When did you start your current job? How long have you worked there? When did the shop open? How long has it been open?

L.h: A Connected to now, or finished?

L.p: The present perfect connects the past with now: the result is still important. The past simple tells us about a finished event, with no connection to the present.

L.e: My bike has been stolen, so I'm walking to work. (= I still don't have it) My bike was stolen last year, but the police found it a week later. I've broken my arm, so I can't play on Saturday. I broke my arm when I was nine.

L.p: We often give news with the present perfect. When we go on to give details – when, where, how – we change to the past simple.

L.e: Have you heard? There's been an accident on the motorway. A lorry crashed into a bridge at about six o'clock. I've cut my finger! I did it while I was opening a tin.

L.p: Questions that ask when or how something happened refer to a finished time, so they take the past simple.

L.e: When did you arrive? What time did the match finish? How did you hurt your back? Where did you buy those boots?

L.x: I *saw* (not *have seen*) her yesterday.

L.p: With a period that continues up to now – *today*, *this week*, *this year*, *recently*, *so far* – use the present perfect. Notice how the same words change: *this morning* is finished in the afternoon.

L.e: I've had two coffees this morning. (it's eleven o'clock now) I had two coffees this morning. (it's evening now) Have you been to the cinema recently? It hasn't rained this month.

L.p: For experiences in a life that is still going on, use the present perfect. For people who are no longer alive, the period is finished, so use the past simple.

L.e: My uncle has visited more than fifty countries. Charles Dickens wrote fifteen novels. Have you ever been to Japan? Did you go to Japan when you were a student?

L.p: Make the past perfect with *had* + the past participle. *had* is the same for every person, and in speech it is often shortened to *'d*.

L.e: I'd finished. She'd left. They hadn't arrived. Had you seen it before?

L.p: When you are talking about the past, use the past perfect for something that happened before that time.

L.e: When we got to the station, the train had already left. I didn't recognise him at first because he'd grown a beard. She was nervous because she hadn't flown before. The museum was closed: we had come on the wrong day.

L.x: When we reached the theatre, the play *had already begun* (not *has already begun*).

L.h: C Past simple or past perfect?

L.p: Compare the order of events. With the past simple, one thing happened after the other. With the past perfect, one thing had happened before the other.

L.e: When I arrived, Kim left. (= I arrived, then she left) When I arrived, Kim had left. (= she left before I arrived, so she wasn't there)

L.p: The past perfect is the 'past' of the present perfect. Compare these pairs.

L.e: I'm not hungry. I've just eaten. I wasn't hungry. I'd just eaten. The house is empty – everybody has gone out. The house was empty – everybody had gone out.

L.p: Make the past perfect continuous with *had been* + *-ing*. In speech, *had* is often shortened to *'d*: *I'd been waiting*, *they'd been talking*.

L.p: Use it for an activity that went on for a period up to a moment in the past, or that had just stopped at that moment. Often there was a result that you could see.

L.e: Her hands were dirty because she'd been gardening. We'd been walking for hours, so our feet were sore. When the manager finally arrived, we'd been waiting for forty minutes. The children were excited – they'd been looking forward to the trip for weeks.

L.h: C Present perfect continuous or past perfect continuous?

L.p: Compare a period up to now and a period up to a moment in the past.

L.e: I've been working hard all day, so I'm tired. (= up to now) I'd been working hard all day, so I was tired. (= up to then) She's been learning Italian for a year. She'd been learning Italian for a year when she moved to Milan.

L.h: D Past continuous or past perfect continuous?

L.p: The past continuous says that something was in progress at that moment. The past perfect continuous says that it had been going on before that moment.

L.h: A have and have got for possession

L.p: For things you own, relationships, illnesses and how people look, you can say *have* or *have got*. *have got* is very common in everyday British English. Questions and negatives are different.

L.e: She's got two older brothers. Have you got a minute? I don't have any cash on me. Ben's got a cold, so he's staying in bed.

L.tip: In the past, use *had* (not *had got*): *I had a bike when I was eight. Did you have a pet when you were little?*

L.p: *have* is also used for many actions: *have breakfast/lunch/dinner*, *have a shower/bath*, *have a rest*, *have a party*, *have a good time*, *have a look*, *have a chat*, *have a baby*. Here you can't use *have got*, but you can use the continuous, and questions take *do/does/did*.

L.e: We usually have lunch at one. Sorry, I can't talk now – I'm having dinner. Did you have a nice weekend? Let's have a look at the map.

L.h: A Things that were true but aren't now

L.p: *used to* + the base form describes habits and situations in the past that are no longer true. It is the same for all persons.

L.e: I used to play the piano, but I gave up when I was twelve. This building used to be a cinema. My dad used to have a beard. We used to spend every Christmas at my aunt's.

L.p: In questions and negatives, use *did* + *use to* (without *-d*).

L.e: Did you use to wear glasses? Where did your family use to live? I didn't use to like olives, but now I love them.

L.x: *Did you use to* (not *Did you used to*) have long hair?

L.p: There is no present form of *used to*. For habits now, use the present simple, often with *usually*. Don't confuse *used to do* with *be used to doing* (= be familiar with), which is in Unit 61.

L.e: I usually walk to work. (not I use to walk) I used to drive to work, but now I walk.

L.x: I *used to* (not *was used to*) smoke, but I stopped years ago.

L.p: For actions that were repeated in the past, you can also use *would*. But *would* is not possible for states.

L.e: Every summer we would go camping in Cornwall. Grandma would sing to us at bedtime. We used to have a dog. (not would have)

L.p: Use *I'll* (= *I will*) when you decide to do something at the moment of speaking. You have not planned it before.

L.p: *will* + the base form gives our opinion or knowledge about the future: what we expect, predict or know will happen.

L.h: B will be doing for things that will happen anyway

L.p: We also use it for things that are already planned or that will happen in the normal course of events. It is a polite way to ask about someone's plans.

L.e: Will you be going past the post office? Could you post this for me? I'll be seeing Tom later, so I can give him your message. The plane will be landing in ten minutes.

L.p: *will have* + past participle looks back from a point in the future: by then, the action is complete.

L.e: By the end of June I'll have finished the course. Next year we'll have been married for twenty years. We're late – the speeches will have finished by the time we arrive.

a: This time tomorrow I will be lying on the beach.
This time tomorrow I'll be lying on the beach.

items.q: By next week I will finished the project.
a: By next week I will have finished the project.

units.O: Imagine a day a year from now. What will you be doing at different times of the day, and what will you have achieved by then?
units.t: will be doing and will have done
units.sub: in progress or completed at a future time

L.h: A Present tense after when, until, as soon as …

L.p: After time words such as *when*, *while*, *before*, *after*, *as soon as*, *until* and *by the time*, and after *if* and *unless*, use a present tense to talk about the future – not *will*.

L.e: Send me a message when you land. Stay in the car until I get back. As soon as the rain stops, we'll go out. Turn the lights off before you leave.

L.x: I'll phone you when I *arrive* (not *will arrive*).
Tell me as soon as you *hear* (not *will hear*) anything.

L.h: B Present perfect: first one thing, then the other

L.p: You can use the present perfect after these words to make it clear that the first action will be finished before the second one happens.

L.e: When I've finished this chapter, I'll make dinner. Don't go until you've signed the form. After you've read the letter, you'll understand.

L.p: Use *if* for something that may or may not happen. Use *when* for something you are sure will happen.

L.e: If it's sunny tomorrow, we'll have a picnic. (= maybe it will be sunny) When the baby wakes up, we'll go for a walk. (= the baby will certainly wake up)
